messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] detection funtion extraction R
messages.body_plain:
Michelle

I understand your intention: you have one complete data set and a second "incomplete" data set. I presume there were no distance measurements made for the auditory detections. You wish to use the detection function derived from the first data set and apply it to the second.

Before discussing how to do that, you must recognise the threats to your inference in doing so. You are making the (untested) assumption that the second data set shares the same detection function as the first. If that assumption is false, this procedure will produce biased estimates. The second challenge involves the measure of uncertainty. In a conventional distance sampling analysis, there is variability in the encounter rate between transects as well as uncertainty in the parameters of the detection function. With this "alternative" analysis, it is not clear how to quantify the uncertainty in the detection function, because there is no fitting associated with the "incomplete" data set. You could use the uncertainty from the detection function fitted to the "complete" data set, but that is probably the wrong uncertainty to use.

With those caveats, you would estimate the encounter rate (number of detections per unit of effort) and the coefficient of variation of that average encounter rate from the "incomplete" survey. In addition, you would "borrow" the detection probability (and its CV) from the detection function fitted to the complete survey. You need not use the Distance​ package to estimate the encounter rate information and its CV. The point estimate of detection probability and its CV can be extracted from the summary of  a dsmodel​ object, for example:

Point estimate:
simply apply the classical distance sampling formula

Precision of point estimate:
apply the delta method approximation, combining the two CVs:
If you have questions about this, feel free to respond.

messages.subject: Distance Sampling in Pangolin Density Estimation
messages.subject_clean: Distance Sampling in Pangolin Density Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
Currently, I am conducting research on Density Estimation of Pangolin (Manis spp.) burrow in Central Nepal. I have chosen Distance Sampling. My study area has an area of 198 hectares. In the study area, the pangolin burrows are distributed in a restricted area (around the source of water). The burrows can be found in around 2-3 hectares only. I have taken 8 line transects of length 400 meters each. With 30meters truncation, a total of 22 burrows have been recorded. I think, in this situation the error would be huge. Burrows being restricted in small area, is it applicable to apply burrow density estimation over the whole area? What can be done to reduce the errors in this situation? I am confused. Any suggestions would be great. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Sailendra Tiwari
Nepal

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance Sampling in Pangolin Density Estimation
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance Sampling in Pangolin Density Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Sailendra

You have asked an interesting sampling question.

You describe two different regions: "study area" of 198ha and "burrow around water" of 2-3ha. Which of those two regions did you sample with your 8 transects (I assume the transects were placed randomly in whichever region you selected)?

If you only placed transects in the region 2-3ha in size, then that is your study area therefore the region to which you are making inference. Alternatively, if you randomly placed your transects within the 198ha region, then your inference is to the 198ha region.

If you did the latter, there is likely to be high variability in encounter rate between transects because transects near water may have had detections, whereas transects not near water were unlikely to have detections. It is not appropriate to apply density of burrows near water to the entire study area, that would be misleading.

You might consider a stratified sampling design, where you delineate a stratum near water and place transects within that region and also a second stratum (not near water) and place transects within that region. You would then analyse the data recognising the stratified nature of the design.  You could consult this example for a description of such a design and analysis:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-2%20Stratification.pdf

As a final comment, I note you seem to be detecting pangolin burrows, rather than pangolins. If you equate the two, you are assuming every burrow is occupied by a pangolin. That seems like an assumption that should be tested.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance Sampling in Pangolin Density Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sailendra,
Just to add to Eric's excellent points, that even if sampling was perfect in terms of survey design and field methods, and 1 burrow = 1 pangolin assumption is valid, only 22 burrows means that there will be high uncertainty regarding the estimation of the detection function, and this uncertainty will propagate to density estimates. We recommend at least 60-80 detections per detection function for reliable density estimates. If you wanted to increase the robustness of the detection function estimation you might conduct additional lines, to increase the number of detections used to estimate the detection function. Since doing the same lines again and again is unlikely to yield independent detections of immobile structures like nests, with most nests detected on subsequent visits of the same line being nests already found on the first visit, you could try to use e.g. 3 sets of equally spaced lines with 3 random orientations, increasing the sample size to, on average, 88 nests, 22 nests for each repetition of the design. Of course this only works if you can assume that the second (and third, forth etc) time you conduct the survey you are not aware of the location of the nests given that you have already found them before. If that is reasonable, you could perhaps turn your density estimate into a more robust one using this strategy.
Cheers
Tiago

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Dsims error for run.simulation
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lisa, Janet and List

This was an issue with observations which occurred across stratum boundaries. In this situation there was a mismatch between the stratum ID's for the individual and the transect resulting in NA values in the Area column which results in the error.

I have now resolved this so detections currently cannot be made across stratum boundaries.

dsims can be installed with these fixes using the following code (we also plan to have dsims back on CRAN with these changes during October)

# First, ensure you have a copy of the devtools package
if (!nzchar(system.file(package = "devtools"))) install.packages("devtools")
# install dsims from github:
devtools::install_github("DistanceDevelopment/ds...@CRAN-1.0.3",
                         build_vignettes = TRUE)

Best wishes,
Laura

Dr. L Marshall

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

University of St. Andrews

Tel: +44 (0)1334 461808

While I may send emails outside of my normal office hours, I have no expectation of a response outside of yours.

Please note that my core working hours are now concentrated between 9am Monday and 2pm Thursday. There may be a delay in my response to emails outwith these times.
